props.title: What a Girl Wants
props.initialSlug: Teen searches for dad, finds royal British identity

sections.content: What a Girl Wants (2003) perfectly captures the early 2000s teen movie renaissance, following the success of The Princess Diaries (2001). Amanda Bynes, fresh from Nickelodeon stardom, brings her signature charm to this modern twist on the fish-out-of-water story. The film cleverly reimagines the 1958 play "The Reluctant Debutante," adding contemporary pop culture touches and father-daughter dynamics that resonated with millennial audiences. It sits comfortably alongside other identity-exploration teen films like Legally Blonde (2001) and Mean Girls (2004).

sections.content: The film's success sparked a wave of transatlantic teen comedies exploring class differences and cultural clashes. Wild Child (2008) and St. Trinian's (2007) followed similar formulas of American attitudes confronting British tradition. Colin Firth's performance as the stuffy-but-loving father Henry Dashwood added gravitas to the genre, much like Mark Harmon in Freaky Friday (2003) and Hugh Grant in About a Boy (2002).

Director Dennie Gordon crafted a visual love letter to London, contrasting modern youth culture with historical aristocracy. The film's fashion choices became particularly influential, with Bynes's bohemian-meets-proper-British style inspiring teen fashion. This aesthetic influence can be traced through later films like Monte Carlo (2011) and The Prince & Me (2004). SUBHEAD: Cultural Impact and Legacy

sections.content: What a Girl Wants solidified Amanda Bynes as a leading teen actress, following her success in Big Fat Liar (2002). The film's exploration of authenticity versus social expectations became a blueprint for later coming-of-age stories like Easy A (2010) and The DUFF (2015). Its soundtrack, featuring Christina Aguilera's "What a Girl Wants" and original songs, exemplified the era's pop-rock teen movie musical tradition.
